title: Jackass: The Movie
full_review:
"Jackass The Movie" (Paramount), derived from the MTV series of the same name, is a sophomoric, vulgar series of vignettes in which a group of failed frat-boy wannabes record about three dozen short incidents of pranks, practical jokes, vandalism, self-torture, abuse, mutilation and other violent acts too repulsive to describe.

There is no plot to this "movie." It is simply an unconnected chronicle of cartoon stunts performed by live actors. However, unlike cartoons violence, the consequences here appear real. People get hurt and their pain is part of the hilarity for the rest of their friends. Repulsive body-fluid excretions are caught on camera, as are bruisings -- and at least one cranial concussion. In cartoons, pratfall injury can be funny because it is not real. When it is real, it is just wretched. It is one thing to watch Wiley Coyote crash into the mesa chasing Road Runner on his Acme rocket skates. It is another to watch it actually happen to a human being.

Producers Johnny Knoxville, Spike Jonze and Jeff Tremaine, who also directed, filmed a group of MTV sketch personalities (including Knoxville, Bam Margera, Chris Pontius, "Steve-O," Dave England, Ryan Dunn and Jason "Wee Man" Acuna) performing gross-out dares and humiliations upon each other. In one episode, electrodes are activated on men's nipples and genitals. In another context, this would be torture but because it is done by friends it's supposed to be funny. A more appropriate and horrified reaction would be "What were they thinking?"

There are other categories of vile skits that involve defecation and rectal exams best left without further elaboration. Less egregious but just plain stupid is when a rental car is returned to the rental agent after it's been wrecked at a demolition derby. There are some harmless jokes, such as blowing air horns to disrupt golfers as they tee off, or running down the streets of Tokyo dressed in panda-bear suits, but these are relative calms before the storms begin again.

There are also some obvious elements of racism against Asians, as many of the pranks are performed at their expense while on tour in Japan. Some of the humor is supposed to derive from Westerners who mock Japanese customs.

Clearly there is a perverse youth culture out there that this film seeks to reflect and exploit. Many in the audience laughed uproariously at "Jackass" or groaned in amused revulsion. Paramount, MTV and Viacom executives who financed and marketed this trash should be ashamed of themselves. For films of this ilk, perhaps Paramount should exchange its now-meaningless pinnacle trademark for some more appropriate corporate symbol, such as a garbage dump.

Because of vulgar body-fluid humor, violent acts of mutilation and torture, some nudity and recurring rough language, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops classification is O -- morally offensive. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
